scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the Malwa area of the Punjab region.
It was historically the 'Babeyan da Gidhha', performed by the elderly men of the community.
It is specifically associated with the districts of Muktsar, Bathinda, Faridkot, Sangrur, Ferozpur, Mansa, and Patiala.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Malwai Giddha is a social dance used for celebration and the expression of folk wit.
The teasing nature of the Boliaan allows for a playful social dynamic within the community.
It serves as a repository of regional Malwai dialect and oral history.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves performers reciting Boliaan, which are folk couplets often used for teasing.
Performers must play instruments in rhythm while dancing.
The technique requires the performer to know how to carry and manipulate specific instruments like the Kato and Chimta while maintaining the beat.
Watch for Kato manipulation.

Formation: Performers stand in a circle; soloists move to the center to deliver verses

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is defined by live instrumentation played by the dancers themselves.
Key instruments include the Tumbi (single-string), Chimta (percussive tongs), Kato (wooden squirrel instrument), and Kartara.
Listen for the Tumbi, Chimta, Kato, Kartara.
The sound is dominated by the metallic jingle of the Chimta and the sharp wooden clacks of the Kato and Sapp, overlaid with high-pitched Tumbi melodies and rhythmic male chanting.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The sources do not name specific individual historical figures, referring instead to the 'Babey' (old men) as the collective originators of the style.
The dance is specific to the Malwa region, distinguishing it from the Majha or Doaba styles of Punjabi folk dance.
Malwai Giddha is a male counterpart to the female Giddha, though it possesses a distinct instrumental and poetic character.
